catalog_quote: There are three tones in Turung, a low tone (marked 1), a high tone (marked 2) and a mid tone (marked 3). ... The same three tones are also analysed for stop final words. ... In addition to the tones that operate at the syllable level, pitch in Turung speech is affected by two other considerations: stress, which is a phrase level phenomenon, and intonation, which is an utterance level phenomenon. ... The phrase level phenomenon of stress is the most challenging for the analysis of the Turung language. The complex interplay between stress and the tonal system requires much more analysis than it has so far received in this study. Given the frequency of iambic (short-long) structures in this language, it is somewhat surprising that at the phrase level, stress appears to fall on the penultimate syllable, provided that syllable is not a minor syllable. ... audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (tonal-OR-pitch accent, domain phrase for the only stress rule) rests on the best available source, a 2010 656-pp. reference grammar with instrumental pitch data, held and quoted verbatim at the cited pages (p. 84, pp. 199-201, p. 216). Glottolog confirms Turung (turu1252) is a dialect of sing1264, so the source is on-target; the 1889 Needham sketch is correctly demoted to secondary and reconciled. Morey 2014 (downloaded now, LD&C 8: 651) refines rather than contradicts: it restates three tones on live and stopped syllables and adds an explicit word-level remark that Turung is 'strongly iambic, with stress on final syllables', consistent with the record's the primary-stress rule note on the 'natural iambic structure of Turung disyllables' and with phrasal stress on the penultimate major syllable. no reclassification needed; at most the the secondary-stress rule could cite Morey 2014:651 for word-internal iambic

sources.citation: Morey, Stephen. 2014. Studying tones in North East India: Tai, Singpho and Tangsa. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 637-671. (ScholarSpace hdl 10125/24619)
sources.quote: 'A further issue in studying the tones in Turung is that a large number of words are not monosyllabic. The language is strongly iambic, with stress on final syllables, making the last syllable usually longer, which allows for more contour movement. ... the study of higher level tones, what we would otherwise term intonation, seems to suggest that intonation overrides tone.' Three contrastive tones on live and on stopped syllables reaffirmed (p. 653).
